stem: In the statement of profit or loss of a trading business, carriage inwards is part of:

options.rationale: Correct: it is a cost of getting the goods ready for sale.
That heading is for carriage outwards and other costs of delivering to customers.
Carriage inwards is a cost of purchasing, so it is not an overhead.
It is a cost, not income.

explanation: Carriage inwards increases the cost of the goods purchased, so it goes in the cost of sales calculation.

stem: Which item is deducted from sales to arrive at revenue?

options.rationale: Correct: goods returned by customers reduce sales.
Returns outwards reduce purchases, not sales.
Discount allowed is an expense.
Carriage outwards is a distribution cost.

explanation: Only returns inwards are deducted from sales; discounts and carriage are shown separately.

stem: How does the statement of profit or loss of a service business differ from that of a trading business?

options.rationale: A service business has many expenses, such as wages and rent.

options.content: It does not show profit for the year
options.rationale: Every business shows its profit for the year.

options.content: It shows drawings as an expense
options.rationale: Drawings are never an expense.

options.content: It has no cost of sales or gross profit
options.rationale: Correct: no goods are bought for resale.

explanation: A service business starts with revenue (fees) and deducts expenses; there is no cost of sales.

stem: Which item would be shown as a distribution cost?

options.rationale: Carriage inwards is part of cost of sales.
Correct: it is the cost of delivering goods to customers.
Office rent is an administrative expense.
Loan interest is a finance cost.

explanation: Distribution costs are the costs of selling and delivering goods to customers.

stem: Opening inventory was US\$6,200, purchases US\$41,300, carriage inwards US\$750, returns outwards US\$900 and closing inventory US\$7,100. What is the cost of sales?

options.rationale: Carriage inwards has been left out.
Returns outwards have been added instead of deducted.
Closing inventory has been added instead of deducted.

hints: Closing inventory is deducted, returns outwards are deducted.

stem: Closing capital of a sole trader is calculated as:

options.content: opening capital + drawings - profit for the year
options.rationale: Drawings reduce capital and profit increases it.

options.content: opening capital - profit for the year + drawings
options.rationale: The signs are reversed.

options.content: opening capital + profit for the year + drawings
options.rationale: Drawings are withdrawn from the business, not added.

options.content: opening capital + profit for the year - drawings
options.rationale: Correct: profit increases capital and drawings reduce it.

explanation: Capital grows by profit retained and shrinks by what the owner withdraws.
hints: What does the owner add and what does the owner take out?

stem: Closing inventory of US\$8,400 was omitted from both statements. What is the effect?

options.content: Gross profit is overstated and total assets are overstated
options.rationale: Without the deduction cost of sales is too high, so gross profit is understated.

options.content: Gross profit is understated but total assets are correct
options.rationale: Inventory is a current asset, so total assets are also understated.

options.content: Gross profit, profit and total assets are all understated
options.rationale: Correct: cost of sales is too high by 8,400 and current assets lack the inventory.

options.content: Profit is correct but current assets are understated
options.rationale: Profit is understated as well because cost of sales is overstated.

explanation: Omitting closing inventory overstates cost of sales and understates gross profit, profit, current assets and capital by the same amount.
hints: Closing inventory is deducted from cost of sales.

stem: In a year a sole trader's profit was US\$14,000 and drawings were US\$17,500. Which statement is the best conclusion?

options.content: Capital has risen by US\$3,500 because drawings are an income
options.rationale: Drawings reduce capital; they are not income.

options.content: Profit must have been misstated because drawings cannot exceed profit
options.rationale: Drawings may exceed profit; it simply reduces capital.

options.content: Capital has fallen by US\$3,500, so the owner is taking out more than the business earned
options.rationale: Correct: closing capital = opening + 14,000 - 17,500.

options.content: Capital is unchanged because drawings are not an expense
options.rationale: Drawings are not an expense but they still reduce capital.

explanation: Capital falls by 3,500 (14,000 - 17,500). Continued withdrawals above profit weaken the business.

stem: A service business has a gross profit figure in its statement of profit or loss.
explanation: False. A service business has no cost of sales, so it has no gross profit; fees are revenue and costs are expenses.

stem: Goods taken by the owner for personal use increase the drawings used to calculate closing capital.
explanation: True. They are recorded as drawings at cost, so closing capital is reduced by them.
hints: The owner has taken value out of the business.

stem: Match each item to the heading under which it appears in the statement of profit or loss.
explanation: Costs of delivery are distribution costs, interest is a finance cost, commission earned is other income and wages of office staff are administrative.

stem: Complete the formula for non-current assets.

payload.template: Carrying amount = cost {{blank:a}} accumulated depreciation, shown within {{blank:b}}.

explanation: Carrying amount is cost less accumulated depreciation and appears under non-current assets.

stem: Name the heading under which interest on a bank loan is shown in the statement of profit or loss.
explanation: Interest on borrowings is a finance cost.

stem: A trader's sales were US\$92,400 and returns inwards US\$1,800. Cost of sales was US\$61,350. Calculate the gross profit.
explanation: Revenue = 92,400 - 1,800 = 90,600; gross profit = 90,600 - 61,350 = 29,250. Ignoring the returns gives 31,050.
workedSolution: 1. Revenue = 92,400 - 1,800 = 90,600; gross profit = 90,600 - 61,350 = 29,250. Ignoring the returns gives 31,050.

stem: A business has gross profit of US\$38,500, discount received of US\$640, expenses of US\$24,900 before depreciation and depreciation of US\$3,200. Calculate the profit for the year.
explanation: 38,500 + 640 - 24,900 - 3,200 = 11,040. Deducting the discount gives 9,760 and omitting depreciation gives 14,240.
workedSolution: 1. 38,500 + 640 - 24,900 - 3,200 = 11,040. Deducting the discount gives 9,760 and omitting depreciation gives 14,240.

stem: At 31 December 2025 a sole trader's total assets were US\$61,400 and total liabilities US\$18,950. Capital at 1 January 2025 was US\$36,000 and drawings during the year were US\$9,420. Calculate the profit for the year.
explanation: Closing capital 61,400 - 18,950 = 42,450. Profit = 42,450 - 36,000 + 9,420 = 15,870. Forgetting drawings gives 6,450.
workedSolution: 1. Closing capital 61,400 - 18,950 = 42,450. Profit = 42,450 - 36,000 + 9,420 = 15,870. Forgetting drawings gives 6,450.
hints: Rearrange: profit = closing capital - opening capital + drawings.

stem: A business had revenue of US\$88,000 and profit for the year of US\$15,870. Calculate the profit margin (profit for the year ÷ revenue × 100) as a percentage to one decimal place.
hints: Use revenue, not cost of sales, as the base.

stem: Explain why the statement of profit or loss of a driving school has no cost of sales.

points.description: A service business does not buy goods for resale
Its costs, such as wages, fuel and rent, are expenses of providing the service

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A driving school sells lessons, not goods, so there is no purchase of inventory to resell. Its costs are expenses of running the business and are deducted from fee revenue.

explanation: One mark for each point.

stem: Distinguish between revenue and other income, giving one example of each.

points.description: Revenue arises from the main activity of the business (e.g. sales of goods or fees)
Other income arises from secondary activities (e.g. commission or discount received)
Both increase profit, but only revenue is used to calculate the gross profit and the profit margin

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Revenue is income from the main trade, such as sales of goods. Other income arises from secondary items, such as commission received or discount received. Revenue is the base for gross profit and the margins; other income is added after gross profit.

explanation: Marks for the definitions with examples and for the use of revenue.
hints: Which items are added after gross profit?

stem: Chipo's profit was US\$9,800 but she took drawings of US\$14,300. Evaluate the effect on the business and advise her.

points.description: Capital falls by US\$4,500 (9,800 - 14,300), so the owner is taking out more than the business earned
The business may have to sell assets or borrow to pay the drawings and may be unable to replace equipment
Drawings may be justified in the short term for personal needs or if earlier profits were retained
Advice: reduce drawings to below profit or raise profit, and keep cash for creditors

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Capital falls by US\$4,500, so Chipo is drawing on the business's past profits. This weakens liquidity and may force borrowing or the sale of assets. It may be acceptable for a short time, but she should reduce drawings to below profit or improve profit.

explanation: One mark each for the figure, the consequence, the balancing point and the advice.
hints: Apply the capital formula, then think about cash.
